results.content: Data fields’ formats, kinds, and restrictions, as well as any rules for working with the data, are often specified in a canonical schema. Canonical Data Model is a **design pattern used in software development for breaking down a data model into its constituent parts** — namely, Identify, Persist, and Domain — to make the model more manageable and testable. ## What is the Canonical Data Model? Canonical data models are **design patterns used to standardize data representation** in various software and hardware environments. * The goal of a canonical data model is to **provide a standard, domain-specific data model that may serve as a guideline for data representation in different kinds of software**. As a result, it may be less of a hassle to integrate and transfer data across apps, and data will be more consistent and compatible across systems.In most cases, the canonical data model pattern is tailored to the requirements of the application area it will be employed. A retail store’s canonical data model, for instance, may define and explain the relationships between customers, items, and orders. * **Using a canonical data model may simplify the process of sharing and integrating data across systems, saving a great deal of time and money.**It’s important to remember that this pattern may be used with a wide variety of data formats and storage mechanisms, such as the canonical data model, which can be used to map not just JSON and XML, but CSV and  SQL databases as well. ## Canonical Data Model structure. The following components are commonplace in every canonical data model:. * The canonical data model also specifies the **connections** between each entity type. * Data integrity and consistency may be maintained by using predefined **constraints** that are defined by the canonical data model. * Canonical data models specify what changes should be made to data before it is transferred across systems. ## FREE TRIAL FOR DEEPCHECKS' LLM EVALUATION SOLUTION**Fill Out Your Details Here**. ## Get a Demo of Deepchecks LLM Evaluation**Fill Out Your Details Here**. ## FREE TRIAL FOR DEEPCHECKS' LLM EVALUATION SOLUTION**Fill Out Your Details Here**.

results.title: Avro Schema Fingerprints · Ambitious Systems
results.content:
Title: Avro Schema Fingerprints · Ambitious Systems
# Avro Schema Fingerprints. Unlike other serialization systems, Avro does not package type information within encoded data. When Avro data is read, the schema used when writing it is always present. There are cases when the schema is packaged along with encoded data. But in many situations, Avro schemas have to be made available separately:. In these instances, it is beneficial to generate a **fingerprint** of the schema that can uniquely identify it instead of relying on an explicit marker or version identifier. ***A "fingerprint" is a shorter bit string that uniquely identifies the original schema.***. This section will step through an example of generating a unique fingerprint of an Avro Schema. ### Schema Fingerprints. To transform a Writer Schema into a fingerprint, we first need to convert the writer's schema into a *Parsing Canonical Form*:. So if the Parsing Canonical Forms of two schemas are textually equal, then those schemas are considered the "same" as far as a reader is concerned. In the Avro context, fingerprints are generated on these Parsing Canonical Forms to guarantee schema usability. * **Rabin** is a small 64-bit CRC fingerprint that guarantees the uniqueness of schema caches of up to a million entries - sufficient for most implementations. * **MD5**: 128-bit fingerprints that come in handy when manipulating tens of millions of schemas. **Note:** We will be using the deprecated avro-python3 package for this example, as the mainstream `avro` package does not have normalization and fingerprinting abilities yet. from avro.schema import parse. We will next generate the Parsing Canonical Form of the writer's schema:. writer_schema_canonical = avro.schemanormalization.ToParsingCanonicalForm(writer_schema). We can then generate a fingerprint of the Canonical Form:. digest = avro.schemanormalization.Fingerprint(writer_schema_canonical, "CRC-64-AVRO"). We can clearly use this fingerprint like a unique identifier to store and retrieve schemas. Any schema that is a variant of this schema will result in the same fingerprint. writer_schema_duplicate_canonical = avro.schemanormalization.ToParsingCanonicalForm(writer_schema_duplicate). digest_duplicate = avro.schemanormalization.Fingerprint(writer_schema_duplicate_canonical, "CRC-64-AVRO"). Analysing the duplicate schema reveals why the same fingerprint is generated. The schema when converted into the Parsing Canonical Form resulted in a structure that is the same as before! The Parsing Canonical Form ensures that the irrelevant details of the Avro schema are ignored, and two schemas that are structurally the same always generate the same fingerprint.

I'm trying to implement a custom `JsonValidator` class which adds more validations on top of what should already be handled by the default validator based on the schema. Particularly, I wouldn't like to check myself whether the value being validated matches the schema before executing the additional checks, which assume it does. I'd like the `Validate()` method being called after the default validation and having an easy way to check whether that validation passed. Or maybe having an option to suppress the call to the custom validator for values that don't match the schema. I didn't find anything in the `JsonValidatorContext` object that helps with this. Following the advice in this post I re-parsed the schema (to get rid of custom validators) and used it to check whether the value matches the schema before executing my custom validations. `public override void Validate(JToken value, JsonValidatorContext context). var defaultSchema = JSchema.Parse(context.Schema.ToString());. Is there a better way? ## 1 Answer 1. Why don't you use `context.Schema` directly ?
